metadata.title: Profiling low-proficiency science students in the Philippines using machine learning

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Philippines sample from PISA 2018, obtained via a two-stage stratified sampling design (random selection of 187 schools across 17 regions, then random selection of students within schools). The manuscript reports the final analytic sample size (7233 students) and describes extensive preprocessing (dropping variables with 100% missingness, kNN imputation with k=7, correlation-based variable removal, and feature scaling). However, it does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the machine-learning training/evaluation. Because the models are standard ML classifiers (Random Forest, SVM, logistic regression, MLP, decision tree) and the paper does not mention weight-aware estimation, the weighting strategy is unclear and may be omitted; this matters because PISA data are clustered by school and weights are typically used to restore population representativeness.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Philippines national sample from PISA 2018 (15-year-olds). The outcome was derived from science proficiency levels using PV1SCIE (first plausible value of science literacy). For modeling, students were categorized into poor-performing (Level 1b and below) vs better-performing (Levels 1a, 2, and above). Data preparation trimmed the dataset by dropping students with >50% missingness across the candidate predictor variables, removing variables with 100% missingness, imputing remaining missing entries using k-nearest neighbor imputation with k=7, removing variables with high correlation (|r|>0.75) to reduce negative suppressors, and scaling/normalizing variables. The final modeling dataset used 80% of data for training and 20% for testing, with class balancing applied only to the training set (SMOTE oversampling for the poor class and Tomek Links undersampling for the better class).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (best): Training precision=0.74, recall=0.79; Test precision=0.73, recall=0.66, accuracy=0.74; AUC=0.83. Grid-search accuracy reported as best for RF (final accuracy=0.74).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Philippines (15-year-olds) Science literacy (PV1SCIE) the study leveraged sense of belonging, perceived student cooperation, bullying experience, work mastery motivation, and smartphone internet access to predict poor science proficiency (Level ≤1b) versus better performance, finding that the Random Forest classifier achieved test accuracy of 0.74 with AUC=0.83. This indicates that non-instructional factors captured in student self-reports (e.g., school connectedness and ICT access) can meaningfully distinguish extremely low science achievers, suggesting that Philippine science interventions should target these learner experiences alongside any curriculum reforms, while noting the model is predictive (not causal) and SHAP-based interpretation does not establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses the Philippines sample from PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) and operationalizes science literacy using PV1SCIE, then converts proficiency into a binary target: poor performers (Level 1b and below) versus better performers (Level 1a and above). After trimming students with >50% missingness, removing variables with 100% missingness, imputing remaining missing values via kNN (k=7), dropping highly correlated predictors (|r|>0.75), and scaling features, the authors train multiple ML classifiers and evaluate them on an 80/20 train-test split. The Random Forest model is selected as best, reaching test precision=0.73, recall=0.66, accuracy=0.74, and AUC=0.83. The top drivers are interpreted using SHAP (15 key variables), emphasizing reading-strategy metacognition, school social experiences (belonging/cooperation/bullying), motivation, and home ICT access. Limitations include the predictive (not explanatory/causal) framing, unclear use of PISA sampling weights, and potential sensitivity to the train-test preprocessing and class-balancing procedure.
